{"result":"# Rust and Memory Safety

Rust is a multi-paradigm language that emphasizes performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety [1][2]. Its syntax will feel familiar to C++ developers, yet it has no garbage collector [2].

Graydon Hoare started Rust in 2006, and Mozilla Research sponsored it from 2009 [2]. It was first publicly released in 2010, with version 1.0 following in 2015 [2].

Memory safety protects programs from bugs such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers [3]. Java achieves this through runtime checks of array bounds and pointer dereferences [3]. By contrast, C, C++, and Fortran allow arbitrary pointer arithmetic without bounds checking, which makes them memory-unsafe [3].

Rust also draws on functional programming, including immutability, higher-order functions, algebraic data types, and pattern matching [1]. In place of classes and inheritance, it offers structs, enums, traits, and methods [1].

Rust shows that a systems language can pursue performance while building memory safety into its core design.
